title: Palindrome Number
directAnswer: Decide if an integer reads the same forwards and backwards — without converting to a string. Negatives are never palindromes (the leading minus has no trailing match), and any non-zero number ending in 0 fails too. The elegant answer reverses only the SECOND HALF of the number and compares it to the first half, so the reversed value never exceeds the original and overflow is impossible.

remember.pattern: Reverse half the digits, compare to the other half
remember.formula:
if x < 0 or (x % 10 == 0 and x != 0): return False
rev = 0
while x > rev:
    rev = rev * 10 + x % 10
    x //= 10
return x == rev or x == rev // 10
rules: **Negatives are never palindromes** — `-121` reversed is `121-`, the minus sign has no partner. Return false immediately.
**Any non-zero number ending in 0 fails** — a palindrome can't start with 0, so `10`, `1230` are out. Only `0` itself survives this rule.

**Reverse only HALF the number** — stop when the leftover `x` is no longer greater than the reversed `rev`. This caps `rev` at half the digits, so it can never overflow even when `x` is near `INT_MAX`.
**Handle odd digit counts** by dropping the middle digit: compare `x == rev` (even length) OR `x == rev / 10` (odd length, middle digit lives in `rev`).
**Avoid the string trick if asked** — `str(x) == str(x)[::-1]` works but the interviewer is testing whether you can do it in pure arithmetic with O(1) space.
whenToUse: Asked to test a numeric property (palindrome, digit pattern) without string conversion
Need O(1) extra space — no array or string buffer allowed
Overflow is a concern and you want to provably stay in range
Working digit-by-digit with `% 10` and `/ 10` feels natural
antiSignals: String conversion is explicitly allowed → `str(x) == str(x)[::-1]` is two lines
You need the actual reversed value (Reverse Integer) → reverse the whole thing and overflow-check
Input is already a string / array of digits → two-pointer compare instead of arithmetic
Arbitrary-precision / BigInteger input → digit array, not int math
remember.takeaway: Reversing only half the number is the trick that turns a potential-overflow problem into a clean O(1)-space comparison. The same 'meet in the middle of the digits' idea reappears in Reverse Integer and any 'is this number symmetric?' question — once you see why `x > rev` is the perfect stopping condition, you own this pattern.

interviewerIntent.testing: Whether you can manipulate a number digit-by-digit with `% 10` and `/ 10`, reason about overflow, and find the half-reversal optimization instead of the obvious full-reversal or string conversion.
interviewerIntent.commonMistake: Reversing the entire number and overflowing on inputs near INT_MAX, or forgetting that negatives and trailing-zero numbers can never be palindromes.
interviewerIntent.toStandOut: Knock out the negative and trailing-zero edge cases in one guard line, then reverse only half the digits using `x > rev` as the stop condition — and explain why that bound makes overflow impossible.

problemStatement:
Given an integer `x`, return `true` if `x` is a palindrome, and `false` otherwise.

An integer is a **palindrome** when it reads the same backward as forward.

For example, `121` is a palindrome while `123` is not.

**Follow-up:** Could you solve it without converting the integer to a string?
constraints: x fits in a 32-bit signed integer
No string conversion in the follow-up variant
understanding: Determine whether the decimal digits of x are symmetric. Sign matters: a leading minus has no mirror, so negatives are out. Leading zeros aren't allowed in integers, so any non-zero multiple of 10 (ending in 0) can't be a palindrome because its reverse would start with 0.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Are negative numbers ever palindromes?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: No. -121 reversed reads 121-, and the minus sign has no matching partner. Return false for all x < 0.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Can I convert the number to a string?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: It works (str(x) == str(x)[::-1]), but the follow-up explicitly asks for a no-string solution — so be ready with the arithmetic approach.

clarifyingQuestions.question: What about overflow when reversing?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Reversing the whole number can exceed INT_MAX for large inputs. Reversing only half the digits keeps the reversed value bounded and avoids overflow entirely.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Is 0 a palindrome?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Yes. 0 reads the same both ways. It's the one number ending in 0 that passes the trailing-zero check.

examples.explanation: 121 reads as 121 from left to right and from right to left.
From left to right it reads -121. From right to left it reads 121-. So it is not a palindrome.
Reads 01 from right to left. A non-zero number ending in 0 can never be a palindrome.

diagrams.title: Picking the right approach
diagrams.caption: The decision tree. Palindrome Number lives on the 'no-string, avoid overflow' branch — reverse half.

approaches.name: Reverse the Whole Number
approaches.whenToMention: Mention first as the intuitive arithmetic answer, then immediately flag its overflow risk to motivate the half-reversal.
hints: A palindrome equals its own reverse. Can you build the reverse of x using only arithmetic, then compare it to the original?
Peel digits off the right with `x % 10`, and push them onto a running `reversed` value with `reversed = reversed * 10 + digit`.
Keep a copy of the original (since the loop destroys x), reverse fully, then check `original == reversed`. But watch: a 10-digit reverse can exceed a 32-bit int.
approaches.complexityReasoning: We process each of the ~log₁₀(n) digits once. Only a couple of integer variables are used, so O(1) space — but the reversed value can overflow 32 bits.
approaches.explanation:
The most direct arithmetic reading of "is x a palindrome?" is "does x equal reverse(x)?". So build the full reverse digit-by-digit and compare.

**How the digit peeling works.** `x % 10` extracts the last digit; `x / 10` (integer division) chops it off. To grow the reversed number we shift its existing digits left by multiplying by 10, then drop the freshly peeled digit into the now-empty ones place: `reversed = reversed * 10 + x % 10`. Repeat until `x` becomes 0 and `reversed` holds the mirror image. Because the original `x` is consumed by the loop, we snapshot it into `original` up front so we have something to compare against at the end.

**Why this is the natural first attempt — and its fatal flaw.** It maps one-to-one onto the definition, which makes it easy to reason about. But it has a real bug on a 32-bit machine: the reverse of a valid `int` can be **larger** than `INT_MAX`. Take `x = 1463847412` — a perfectly legal 32-bit int. Its reverse `2147483641`... is fine, but `x = 2147447412` reverses past the 2³¹−1 ceiling and overflows to a garbage negative number, producing a wrong answer (or undefined behavior in C/Java where ints wrap silently).

**The mitigations and why they're unsatisfying.** You can store the reverse in a 64-bit `long` to dodge overflow, but that quietly assumes a wider type is available and feels like papering over the real issue. The cleaner fix — the one interviewers want — is to never build a number bigger than half of `x` in the first place. That's the next approach.
approaches.insight: `reversed = reversed * 10 + x % 10` is the universal 'reverse a number' idiom — memorize it. The catch nobody mentions until it bites them: reversing a full 32-bit int can overflow 32 bits, so either widen to `long` or, better, only reverse half.

Palindrome iff the number equals its own full reverse.

edgeCases.behavior: Negative guard returns false before any reversing.
Reversing in a 32-bit int overflows — this is exactly why we store reversed in a long, or switch to the half-reversal approach.

pitfalls: Reversing into an `int` instead of a `long` — overflows on large 32-bit inputs.
Forgetting to snapshot the original before the loop destroys x.
Not handling negatives — `-121 % 10` is language-dependent and can produce surprising signs.

approaches.name: Reverse Half the Number (Optimal)
approaches.whenToMention: The answer they want. Phrase it as 'reverse the second half and compare to the first half' — and call out why it can't overflow.
hints: You don't need the whole reverse — a palindrome's second half, reversed, equals its first half. Can you build only the reversed second half and stop halfway?
Peel digits into `reversed` while shrinking `x`. The natural stopping point is when `reversed` becomes ≥ `x`: at that moment you've consumed the right half and `x` holds the left half.
For even digit counts, compare `x == reversed`. For odd counts the middle digit ends up in `reversed`, so also accept `x == reversed / 10` (drop that middle digit).
approaches.complexityReasoning: We process only half the ~log₁₀(n) digits, still O(log₁₀ n) time. `reversed` never exceeds half the digits of x, so it stays within range — provably no overflow, O(1) space.
approaches.explanation:
Instead of reversing the entire number and risking overflow, reverse only the **second half** and compare it to the first half. The two halves of a palindrome are mirror images, so the reversed second half should exactly equal the untouched first half.

**The two guard clauses do real work.** First, `x < 0` → false, because a leading minus can never mirror. Second, `x % 10 == 0 && x != 0` → false: a number ending in 0 would need to *start* with 0 to be symmetric, but integers have no leading zeros — so `10`, `1230`, `100` are all immediately disqualified. The lone exception is `0` itself, which is why the guard explicitly spares `x != 0`. Knocking these out up front keeps the main loop clean.

**Why `while (x > reversed)` is the perfect stopping condition.** Each iteration moves one digit from the right end of `x` onto `reversed`, so `x` shrinks and `reversed` grows. They cross exactly at the midpoint of the digits. When `x` becomes less than or equal to `reversed`, we've peeled off the entire right half — `reversed` *is* the reversed second half and `x` *is* the first half. Because we never push more than half the digits into `reversed`, its value is bounded by roughly √(original) in magnitude and **cannot overflow**, even for inputs hugging `INT_MAX`. That's the whole point of this approach.

**Handling odd vs even digit counts.** With an even count like `1221`: the loop ends with `x = 12`, `reversed = 12`, and `x == reversed` → palindrome. With an odd count like `12321`: the loop ends with `x = 12`, `reversed = 123` — the middle digit `3` got swept into `reversed`. We don't care about the middle digit (it mirrors itself), so we strip it with integer division: `reversed / 10 == 12 == x` → palindrome. Accepting `x == reversed || x == reversed / 10` covers both cases in one return.
approaches.insight: The stopping condition `x > reversed` is the elegant core: it self-terminates at the digit midpoint without ever counting the digits first, and it guarantees `reversed` stays small enough to never overflow. Reverse *half*, not the whole — that single idea is what separates the textbook answer from the interview-grade one.

Move the rightmost digit of x onto reversed, building the reversed second half.
Even length: x == reversed. Odd length: drop the middle digit with reversed / 10.

Self-terminating midpoint condition — no need to count digits, and reversed_num never overflows.
Append x's last digit to the reversed second half.

diagrams.title: Where the two halves meet
diagrams.caption: x shrinks from the left, reversed grows from the right; they cross at the middle.

edgeCases.behavior: Guard spares it (x != 0). Loop never runs (0 > 0 is false), returns 0 == 0 → true.
Odd length. Loop ends with x = 12, reversed = 123. x == reversed/10 → 12 == 12 → true.
x % 10 == 0 and x != 0 → guard returns false immediately.

pitfalls: Forgetting the `reversed / 10` clause — breaks every odd-length palindrome like 12321.
Dropping the `x != 0` part of the guard — would wrongly reject 0.
Using `x >= reversed` instead of `x > reversed` — overshoots the midpoint on some inputs.

commonMistakes: Treating negative numbers as possible palindromes — they never are.
Reversing the full number into a 32-bit int and overflowing on large inputs.
Forgetting the odd-length case, so 12321 is reported as not a palindrome.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Overflow from reversing the whole number
commonMistakesDetailed.why: On a 32-bit machine, reversing a valid int can exceed INT_MAX and wrap to garbage. Reverse only half, or use a 64-bit type.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Missing the odd-length comparison
commonMistakesDetailed.why: For odd digit counts the middle digit lands in `reversed`. Comparing only `x == reversed` rejects valid palindromes like 12321.
commonMistakesDetailed.good: return x == reversed_num or x == reversed_num // 10

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Not disqualifying trailing-zero numbers
commonMistakesDetailed.why: A non-zero number ending in 0 (10, 1230) can't be a palindrome. Without the guard the half-reversal logic still works, but stating the rule shows you understand leading-zero impossibility.
